sentence: Linear probes recover Othello-GPT's board with high accuracy, and editing along probe directions changes the model's legal-move predictions.
Neither fact shows that a frozen probe captures every residual-stream distinction the network uses.
We study one 8-layer Othello-GPT, one frozen 64-square linear board probe, and residual edits at `blocks.6.hook_resid_mid` that lie in the kernel of the probe's class-logit contrasts.
Each edit starts from the Editor A reference activation, which is the natural recipient activation after a full-space board editor, with its manifold penalty off, has been applied.
Kernel steps of similar length barely move the output at a natural donor activation.
The edit leaves the probe's 64×3 probability tensor at that reference unchanged to within \(2.2\times10^{-14}\).
On 48 recipient–target pairs, kernel directions taken from the intended target's natural activation raised a legal-mass response score more than wrong-target and random kernel directions.
This held at matched residual L2 and again when every direction was scaled to the same output Jensen–Shannon divergence (0.01) from the Editor A reference.
At matched divergence the advantage over wrong targets was small (\(+0.0266\), 95% interval \([0.0179, 0.0357]\)).

A 64-component ridge map from symbolic board features, trained only on training games, produced an advantage on 48 new pairs without using the target's activation at evaluation (\(+0.0201\) versus wrong targets).
Mean scores nevertheless stayed negative: the learned edit left more probability on moves that should have become illegal than on moves that should have become legal in 47 of 48 pairs.
About 56% of the map's mean gain over Editor A was already obtained by a map that sees only player and occupancy.
On a fresh cohort, both target-switching contrasts were positive on average, but both were positive together in only 13 of 32 triplets, below a preregistered 60% gate.
Those two cohorts are the only fresh samples.
The positive results reuse validation pairs.
A factorial test of visible–kernel interaction gave estimates near zero.

The evidence supports a narrow conclusion: this frozen probe does not exhaust the residual information that affects legal-move outputs, part of the remainder is predictable from symbolic state, and the recovered map is not a transferable board state.
The matched-L2, matched-divergence, and donor-free results are recomputed from saved arrays in the accompanying package.
The ablation, switching, and factorial results are archival values whose arrays were not available for recomputation.
A linear probe that reads the board from Othello-GPT is easy to treat as a description of what the model knows.

Li et al. (2023) trained a GPT-style network on legal Othello move sequences, showed that nonlinear probes recover the board, and showed that editing the probed representation changes which moves the network treats as legal.
Nanda, Lee, and Wattenberg (2023) then showed that a player-relative linear probe is enough to read the board, and that adding probe directions is enough to steer play.
Those results give a causal role to a decoded board.
They do not show that one frozen probe is a complete causal summary of the residual stream.
Probing and intervention answer different questions.
A probe asks whether a feature is linearly readable.
An intervention asks whether a specified change to an activation changes the frozen network's output.
Elazar et al. (2021) made the gap explicit by removing linearly readable information and measuring behavior; high probe accuracy did not imply that the probed feature was what the model used.
The complementary experiment adds information that the probe cannot see, holds the probe's readout fixed, and asks whether behavior still moves.
We run that experiment on the Nanda redistribution of Othello-GPT, an 8-layer Transformer with residual width 512.
We freeze a 64-square multinomial linear probe at the last real token of `blocks.6.hook_resid_mid`.
The probe's independent class-logit contrasts define a rowspace and a complementary nullspace.
Adding a nullspace vector to an activation leaves every square's probe probabilities at that activation unchanged, up to floating-point error.
We call such an edit probe-preserving relative to this probe.
The phrase does not mean that no decoder could read the change, and it does not mean that the model has a second hidden board.
Every edit in this paper is applied to a specific reference activation, and the choice matters.
For a recipient position we write \(h_R\) for its natural activation.

Editor A, a full-space residual editor from earlier work on this model, moves \(h_R\) toward the intended target board as read by the probe; we call its output \(h_E\) the Editor A reference activation.
Its manifold penalty was off.
A natural activation from a position that actually has the target board is \(h_D\).
The final patched activation is \(h_E + t\,\delta\) with \(\delta\) in the probe nullspace.
Probe preservation and the output-divergence calibration are both measured against \(h_E\), not against \(h_R\).
The experiments therefore ask a specific question.
Start from an activation whose probe readout has already been pushed toward the target board.
Can directions that this probe cannot see shift legal-move probability further toward the target, and do they do so more for the intended target than for other boards?
The output measure is a difference of probability masses.

For a recipient position with legal set \(L_r\) and an intended target with legal set \(L_t\), \(G\) is the model's probability on moves that became legal, \(Q\) is its probability on moves that became illegal, and \(Y=G-Q\).
A higher \(Y\) means probability moved toward the target's legal set and away from the recipient's.
It is not move accuracy, and a higher \(Y\) is not a claim that the model now plays the target board.
We ask three questions.
First, do nullspace directions taken from the target's natural activation change \(Y\) more than wrong-target and random nullspace directions?
We answer under two different strength controls, matched residual L2 and matched output Jensen–Shannon (JS) divergence.
Second, can a map that sees only symbolic features of the target produce a comparable nullspace direction without the target's activation at evaluation?
Those features are player-relative occupancy, the legal-move mask, the player to move, and the game stage.
Third, how far does that map go?
We report how much of its gain is already present in a stage-only map.

We also report two tests that a transferable board state would be expected to pass and that this map failed: reliable switching between two targets on the same recipient, and an interaction between independently set visible and nullspace components.
The contribution is empirical and narrow.
We do not propose a theory of Transformer decisions.
We do not claim that every board probe would miss this information, or that the 64-component map recovered the model's decision state.
The experiments support three statements about this probe and this model.
Directions that the probe cannot distinguish still carry some target-aligned influence on legal-move predictions.
Part of that influence can be predicted from symbolic state without a target activation at evaluation.
The resulting edit is far from complete state transfer.
Probing treats a decoder's success as evidence that a representation contains a variable, and the methodological literature has long warned that readout is not use.
Hewitt and Liang (2019) introduced control tasks that a probe can solve without tracking linguistic structure.
Belinkov (2022) surveyed the gap between encoding and causal role.
Elazar et al. (2021) used iterative nullspace projection (Ravfogel et al., 2020) to remove a property and then asked whether behavior changed.
Belrose et al. (2023) gave a closed-form linear erasure method with a guarantee against all linear classifiers.

Ravfogel, Prasad, Linzen, and Goldberg (2021) used the same rowspace–nullspace split to build counterfactuals: their AlterRep method changes the rowspace component of a probe-identified feature, keeps the nullspace component, and measures the change in word predictions.
Those papers remove or alter what a probe reads.
Our edits do the reverse: they keep what the probe reads and change the rest.
The papers above do not ask whether the orthogonal complement of a particular frozen probe still carries target-specific causal influence.
Othello-GPT is the setting in which world-model claims have been examined most carefully.
Li et al. (2023) argued that a network trained only on move tokens maintains an internal board, using nonlinear probes and interventional edits.
Nanda et al. (2023) showed that a player-relative linear basis makes the board linearly readable and steerable by vector addition.
Hazineh, Zhang, and Chiu (2023) intervened along linear board representations layer by layer and found causal use concentrated in the middle layers.
Those interventions move the model along the probe.
Moving along the probe cannot tell us whether the probe is a sufficient statistic for legal-move behavior; that question requires moving within its kernel.
Two later Othello studies make the readout-versus-use distinction in other designs.
Jacopin (2026) reproduced the linear player-relative board in a masked-diffusion language model trained on the same data.
The representation transferred but was weaker, and a Li/Nanda-style board intervention had only a small, inconsistent effect relative to an autoregressive control.
That study asks whether a readable world model is used under a different training objective.
It does not freeze a probe and edit in that probe's kernel.

Lin, JackS, Karvonen, and Can (2024), in a research note that has not been peer reviewed, report that Othello-GPT appears to compute legality through many localized heuristics, including neurons that respond to game stage.
That account is compatible with our finding that a stage-only map carries much of the mean gain, but it is not a nullspace test of a frozen probe.

Activation steering in language models adds residual directions derived from contrastive prompts or trained readers (Turner et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024), usually with a strength coefficient.
We instead match the output divergence of several directions, including wrong-target directions, so that a direction cannot look better merely by disrupting the next-move distribution more.
That is a matching condition, not a new steering algorithm.
Makelov, Lange, Geiger, and Nanda (2024) show that a subspace intervention can activate pathways that are dormant on natural inputs, which is the relevant caution for edits at \(h_E\).
Causal abstraction and distributed alignment search (Geiger et al., 2024, 2025) ask whether a high-level causal variable aligns with a distributed subspace under interchange interventions.
We do not fit such an alignment and make no faithfulness claim.
Our estimand is the change in \(Y\) under an explicitly constructed residual edit.
It is a causal effect of that intervention, not evidence that we found the variable the network uses.
The closest prior statement is that linear board features in Othello-GPT are readable and steerable, while probes in general are not causal summaries.

The design here differs from AlterRep in direction: AlterRep changes the rowspace and keeps the nullspace, and these experiments keep the probe readout and change the nullspace, with wrong-target and random controls and with the completeness tests reported whether they pass or fail.
That description is not a claim that no earlier paper did something similar.

The model is the TransformerLens conversion of Nanda's 8-layer Othello-GPT (\(d_{\mathrm{model}}=512\), 8 heads, vocabulary 61, context 59) trained on synthetic legal self-play following Li et al. (2023).

From the saved singular values, 124 exceed \(10^{-8}\) times the largest, so the rowspace has dimension 124 and the nullspace has dimension 388.
The saved nullspace projector \(P_N\) has trace 388, is idempotent to \(10^{-15}\), and has eigenvalues within \(10^{-14}\) of 0 or 1.
The projector was built so that \(W P_N=0\).
The matrix \(W\) is not in this package, so that product is not recomputed here.

The Editor A reference activation \(h_E\) is the output of Editor A applied to \(h_R\) with the target's player-relative board as its objective.

The natural donor activation \(h_D\) is the model's activation at the target position itself.
The correct-target nullspace direction is \(\delta_{\mathrm{correct}}=P_N(h_D-h_E)\).
A wrong-target direction is \(P_N(h_W-h_E)\) for a wrong-target donor \(h_W\) with the same player and similar occupancy, legal-set size, and prefix length.
A random direction is \(P_N\) applied to a seeded Gaussian vector.
The final patched activation is \(h_E+t\,\delta\).
The probe's readout at \(h_E+t\,\delta\) equals its readout at \(h_E\).

It does not equal the readout at \(h_R\): in the matched-divergence study the probe tensors at \(h_E+t\,\delta\) and \(h_R\) differ by at least 0.93 in some entry for every intervention, because Editor A has already changed the decoded board.

The selected \(k\) is the largest value on that grid, and the cross-validated \(R^2\) was still higher there than at the next smaller value.

The oracle was computed only after the learned directions were frozen.

**Token mapping.** Square \(s\in\{0,\dots,63\}\) in row-major order maps to token \(s+1-c(s)\), where \(c(s)\) is the number of center squares (27, 28, 35, 36) below \(s\).

**Editor A.** Editor A minimizes a board-decoding loss for the target's player-relative labels under the frozen probe, starting from \(h_R\), with an L2 budget of 16, 40 steps, learning rate 0.4, and norm penalty 0.01.
Its output is the Editor A reference activation \(h_E\).
Editor A decoded the exact target board on 22 of the 48 SPEC pairs and on 24 of the 48 NST pairs.
Its logits are bitwise identical in the SPEC and matched-divergence archives, so both studies share the same reference.

**Wrong-target and random directions.** Each SPEC pair has three wrong-target donors with the same player and with occupancy, legal-set size, and prefix length matched within a slack of 4, selected by frozen seeds before any \(Y\) was computed.
Random directions are \(P_N g\) for seeded Gaussian \(g\).
In SPEC, all six controls are rescaled to the correct direction's L2 norm, to relative error \(8\times10^{-16}\).
In the matched-divergence study, each is scaled independently to JS 0.01 from \(h_E\).
The first grid point with JS at least 0.01 is bisected 16 times against its predecessor.
A direction that cannot reach 0.01 fails and remains in the attempt record.
No direction failed in the matched-divergence or NST studies, except the gradient baseline, which calibrated on 7 of 48 pairs.

**Preregistered gates.** SPEC required a mean correct-minus-wrong contrast of at least 0.05 with interval above zero, \(\Delta G>0\) and \(\Delta Q<0\) relative to wrong directions, and a correct-minus-random contrast with interval above zero.
The matched-divergence study required 44 of 48 complete pairs, a mean correct-minus-wrong contrast of at least 0.02, both intervals above zero, \(\Delta G>0\), and \(\Delta Q<0\).

NST required a learned-minus-wrong contrast of at least 0.01, intervals above zero against wrong, random, stage-mean, and Editor A, and the intended \(\Delta G\) and \(\Delta Q\) signs relative to Editor A.
SEM required an incremental advantage of at least 0.01 with interval above zero.

FRESH required at least 29 of 32 complete triplets, \(A_T\) and \(A_W\) of at least 0.005 with intervals above zero, a positive mean of \(C=A_T+A_W\), and both contrasts positive on at least 60% of triplets.
The archival mean of \(C\) was \(+0.0471\) (\([0.0316, 0.0629]\)); the protocol states that a positive \(C\) alone is not bidirectional switching.
VNF required at least 29 of 32 complete triplets, \(I_T\) and \(I_W\) of at least 0.005 with intervals above zero, and random and label-shuffled controls that do not reproduce that pattern.
Because the interaction floor was not met, the control condition does not affect the outcome.
**Bootstrap.** Clusters are recipient games, taken in order of first appearance, resampled with replacement using NumPy's default generator.
The statistic is the mean of cluster means, and intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.
Seeds are 82 plus a metric offset; NST subgroups add 10, 20, 30, or 40.
FRESH and VNF used seeds 9482 and 10482 with 5000 replicates.
